extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters of New York (historical); framers, legislators, and students of constitutional design and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for designing and evaluating a constitution so that legislative, executive, and judicial powers remain separate, checked, and balanced, and for assessing institutional devices (appeals to the people, periodical censors, federal structure, election rules) intended to preserve those limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (distinct departments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, executive, and judiciary departments should be separate and distinct so that no person should exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere written demarcation on parchment is insufficient; institutional arrangements must ensure that members of each department have a will of their own and minimal agency in appointing members of the others. Appointments, modes of selection, tenure, and independence should be arranged to make departments independently able to resist encroachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of concentration of powers / elective despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrating legislative, executive, and judicial powers in the same hands constitutes despotic government; an 'elective despotism' (many elected rulers exercising all powers) is equally dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plurality of hands does not mitigate oppression (e.g., 'one hundred and seventy-three despots would surely be as oppressive as one'). Constitutional design must prevent any single body from exercising the powers of the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention of legislative usurpation of executive and judicial functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature must not assume executive or judicial powers (for example, deciding rights that should be left to judiciary or directing the executive during its sessions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the legislature provides subsistence or varying salaries to judges or subsumes judicial causes within legislative cognizance, it invites encroachment. Watch for laws that alter procedural safeguards (e.g., printed bills for public consideration) or substitute legislative determinations for judicial controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and executive independence from legislative control (emoluments and tenure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges and executives must be as independent as possible from the legislature with respect to emoluments and continuance in office (fixed salaries, secure tenure) to secure their independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the executive or judiciary depend on the legislature for pay or continuation, their independence is nominal. Constitutional provisions (e.g., fixed judicial salaries) are important structural safeguards against legislative pressure or manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about appeals to the people (occasional conventions) as remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a constitutional road to appeal to the people (calling a convention when large majorities of branches agree) is attractive in theory but has serious objections as a general remedy for department encroachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections include: (1) does not address combinations of two departments against the third; (2) frequent appeals imply defects and undermine reverence for government; (3) appeals risk being decided by popular passion and pre-existing parties rather than reason; (4) conventions will often be dominated by those with ties to the legislative branch and thus capture the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of periodical appeals / censorial bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodical appeals (e.g., septennial Councils of Censors) intended to review and correct constitutional infractions are ineffective and risky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical example: Pennsylvania's Council of Censors (1783–84) was split into fixed parties, often comprised of recent office-holders and partisan leaders; their decisions were sometimes misconstrued, lacked effect on legislative practice, and in at least one instance were denied by the legislature. Remoteness of review, entrenched abuses, and party bias undercut utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior structural design as primary safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Because exterior provisions (occasional/periodical appeals, declarations) are inadequate, the internal structure of government must be contrived so constituent parts keep each other in proper places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design departments so that their mutual relations create natural checks: independent modes of election/appointment, varied principles of action, and institutional incentives that lead officials to defend their department's constitutional rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize interdependence in appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of each department should have as little agency as possible in appointing members of the other departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideally, all appointments would be drawn independently from the people through channels with no communication; practical deviations are permissible but the principle should be rigorously observed where feasible (with some relaxation for judiciary where qualifications and permanence matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rival interests to constrain ambition ('ambition must be made to counteract ambition')
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional design should bind private interest to public constitutional rights so that individual ambition and interest operate as checks upon one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create opposite and rival interests within the system (e.g., separate branches with distinct powers and incentives) so that each actor has personal motives to resist encroachments by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide the legislature into different branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Because legislative authority necessarily predominates in republican government, the legislature should be divided into different branches with different modes of election and principles of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different modes of election, terms, constituencies, and responsibilities reduce coordination and make dangerous encroachments harder. Further safeguards (e.g., fortifying the executive) may be necessary where the legislative predominance is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortify the executive (qualified connection to a weaker legislative branch)
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive, being a weaker department, may require fortification—possibly by a qualified connection with the weaker branch of the legislature—to defend its constitutional rights without being detached from legislative accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An absolute negative may be unsafe or insufficient; consider institutional links that encourage the weaker legislative branch to support executive constitutional prerogatives while preserving checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism as double security
rubrics_metrics.description: In a compound republic (federal system), power surrendered by the people is divided between two governments and then subdivided among departments, creating a double security for rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different governments (federal vs. state) will control each other while each subdivides authority internally; this multiplicity of checks complements departmental checks and increases protection against oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect minorities through multiplicity of interests and sects
rubrics_metrics.description: To guard one part of society against injustice by another, the society should be divided into many interests and sects so that an unjust combination of a majority is unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods exist: create a power independent of society (hereditary/self-appointed) or enlarge the multiplicity of interests within society. The latter is preferable in a republic; extent of territory and population increases the number and diversity of interests, reducing the risk of majoritarian injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of an extended republic for self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: A larger society, within a practical sphere, is more capable of self-government because it will encompass a greater number of interests and sects, which prevents oppressive majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judicious federal principle permits a practicable enlargement of the republic while preserving local representation, thereby enhancing stability and protection of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the right of suffrage and election qualifications (House of Representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution should define qualifications of electors and elected for the House: electors to follow the State standard for the most numerous branch; representatives must be at least 25 years old, seven years a U.S. citizen, inhabitant of the electing state at election, and hold no office under the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffrage qualifications are a fundamental article of republican government and should not be left to Congress or the States to vary in ways that would render federal dependence on people ambiguous. These limitations open the house to merit regardless of wealth, religion, or profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of elections to preserve dependence on the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent elections (e.g., biennial) help secure the branch's immediate dependence on and sympathy with the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The precise frequency is not mathematically derivable and depends on circumstances; experience suggests more frequent elections better secure dependence, but practical trade-offs exist. Biennial elections are defended as balancing responsiveness with practicability.
